title: My pre-registered paper test failed at trade 100, and the one "winning" token turned out to be luck
author: Interesting_Gold_792
selftext:
I run paper trading lanes with a team of AI agents. Each lane gets its pass/fail rule written before trade one.

  
H1 traded 6 Solana tokens. Its early-stop rule said: stop at 100 trades if the average after costs is negative. It stopped: 31 wins out of 100, −$351.12 at real cost.

  
But one token, JUP, was up +$96 over 12 trades. Instead of building a new strategy around it, I pre-registered a follow-up test:

* Out of sample (Feb 2024 – Aug 2026, data never used to build H1): 1,209 trades, −0.21% per trade, below the random-entry median.
* JUP had simply outperformed while SOL fell \~25% over the same window.
* Odds that the best of 6 tokens looks this good by chance alone: 20–46%.

Verdict: drift, not edge. No new lane.

  
How do you handle a "winning pocket" inside a failed test?

  
Paper only, not financial advice.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: writing the follow-up test down before touching more data is the whole trick. most people find their JUP and spend the next month building a strategy around one token's year.

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body: Yeah, that was the part I almost skipped. JUP looked good enough that I wanted it to be real. Having the follow-up rules written first made it a lot easier to accept when it didn't hold up. Now any token that looks good inside a failed test gets the same treatment before I build anything on it.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: same here with a bot that has one great week, it gets rerun on dates it never saw before I believe it. that habit is partly why I made Quantradin (quantradin.com), you write the rule in plain words before looking and it runs on paper money where you can't nudge it after the fact.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: That's the right way to handle it. A winning pocket inside a failed test is usually a hypothesis, not a result, and the best of six will often look good just by chance, as your 20 to 46% shows. I'd only chase a pocket if it was named before the test and holds on data you never touched. Splitting a failed test into smaller groups until one wins is how many bad strategies get made. Cymetica's Backtest Labs holds out the last part of the history, which suits this kind of follow-up check.

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body: Agreed, that's how I treat it now. A pocket only gets a follow-up if the follow-up rules are written down first, and it has to hold on data it never touched. If it doesn't, it gets dropped, no second round of slicing.

comments.author: zulfi001
comments.body: good call not building a lane on JUP. ive had the same thing happen a bunch, an idea fails overall but one coin or one stretch of time looks great. what helped me was running the exact same rule unchanged on the other coins and splitting the result by time period. if all the profit comes from one coin or one 3 month window its almost always a single episode, not an edge. the ones that held up for me were the boring ones that showed up a bit everywhere, not big in one place

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body: That matches what I keep seeing. Most of the pockets that look great end up being one coin or a couple of big days doing all the work. Running the same rule untouched on other coins and splitting by period is basically my checklist now before I take anything seriously. The boring "a bit everywhere" point is a good one, I'm going to start treating that as the bar instead of the size of the best result.
